implementation_notes: Scala's standard library supplies the completion contract rather than an event loop: Future is a handle for an operation's result, an ExecutionContext decides where completion callbacks and combinators run (the global one is a ForkJoinPool sized to the processors), and onComplete, foreach, map and flatMap compose continuation-style handlers. Blocking is discouraged, so the dispatcher is the execution context plus the JDK executor underneath, while actual asynchronous I/O still comes from NIO.2 or a framework. Effect-system runtimes such as cats-effect and ZIO add fiber-based async runtimes with true completion semantics, but their effect model is a different abstraction layer.
code_sketch:
import scala.concurrent.{ExecutionContext, Future}
import ExecutionContext.Implicits.global

val session: Future[Session] = Future { connect() }   // runs on the EC
session.onComplete {                                   // completion handler
  case Success(s) => s.send("ok")
  case Failure(e) => log.error("connect failed", e)
}
pitfalls: Blocking inside a Future occupies a ForkJoinPool thread; without blocking{} or a dedicated ExecutionContext the global pool can be starved.
Callbacks run on arbitrary pool threads with no ordering guarantee, so shared mutable state must be synchronised.
A Future is eager and memoised: creating it starts the work, and abandoning it does not cancel the computation.
onComplete needs an implicit ExecutionContext; the compiler error is the only reminder that the dispatch policy matters.
